_comment: Whole concepts Cambridge 0097 requires at Stage 6 that the source pack never contained. Authored from the supplied Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6 and Learner's Book 6, in the voice the units already use. Each one EXTENDS the subject of the unit it joins - the materials unit gains the temperature-and-dissolving work it stopped short of, the electricity unit gains parallel circuits and heat conduction, the ecosystems unit gains what happens when a poison enters a food chain. Nothing here starts a topic its unit does not already cover; the objectives that would need a NEW unit (rocks, soils, the rock cycle, the Solar System, the Moon, light, puberty and the reproductive system) are still recorded in the manifest's gaps and in _needsNewUnit below.
_vehicle: concepts, appended to the unit's own array and rendered by the shell as 'The lesson'. APPENDED and never inserted, because the shell renders in array order and inserting would move every later concept under a learner mid-unit. Safe on a live course: complete('lesson') fires on a button press rather than on a count of concepts, and complete() is add-only, so a learner who marked the lesson studied keeps the tick.

These would fit Unit 1, which is a body-systems unit, and they are NOT authored here deliberately: what a school teaches about puberty and reproduction, and at what age, is a policy decision for the owner and the schools rather than something to slip into a live course unannounced. Flagged for a decision, not blocked on evidence.

concepts.title: Germs, and How Your Body Fights Them
concepts.explanation:
You have met the systems that keep you alive. Now meet the things that try to make you ill, and the defences you already carry against them.

Most illnesses that spread from person to person are caused by living things far too small to see, which we call microorganisms or germs. There are four kinds worth knowing. Bacteria are single living cells; most are harmless and some are useful, like the ones that turn milk into yoghurt, but a few cause illnesses such as cholera and some chest infections. Viruses are much smaller still and are not really alive on their own - they can only copy themselves inside your cells, which is what a cold, measles and influenza do. Fungi cause skin problems like ringworm and athlete's foot. Parasites are larger organisms that live on or in another body, and the malaria parasite, carried between people by mosquitoes, is the one that matters most in much of Africa.

These germs travel in a few well-known ways: in water that has been contaminated, in food that has been badly handled or left warm too long, and in the tiny droplets that leave your nose and mouth when you sneeze, cough or speak. Some travel in blood or other body fluids, and some, like the malaria parasite, are carried by an insect.

Because the routes are known, they can be blocked, and that is what hygiene is. Washing your hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet removes germs that would otherwise travel from your hands to your food. Boiling water that may not be clean kills the germs in it - a filter takes out the dirt you can see and does nothing to the germs. Covering your mouth with your elbow rather than your hand when you cough stops the droplets reaching other people without putting them on the hand you are about to shake. Keeping cooked food covered and cool slows the bacteria that were already on it. Sleeping under a treated net stops the mosquito reaching you at all.

And if a germ gets past all that, your body is not defenceless. Your skin is a barrier that unbroken keeps almost everything out, which is why a cut is worth cleaning. The acid in your stomach is strong enough to kill most of what you swallow. Your nose, windpipe and lungs are lined with sticky mucus that traps dust and germs, and tiny hairs that sweep the mucus back up to be swallowed - the same mucus you met in the respiratory system, doing a second job. These defences work every day without you noticing, and the reason you are not ill more often is that they are working now.
concepts.example: A family in a village boils their drinking water and sleeps under nets, and the children still catch colds at school. That is not a failure of the hygiene: boiling blocks the water route and nets block the mosquito route, and a cold travels by neither - it arrives in droplets from another child a metre away. Each measure blocks one route, so you need the measure that matches the route.

concepts.title: When a Poison Travels Up a Food Chain
concepts.explanation:
You know that energy passes along a food chain, from the producer to the animal that eats it and on to the animal that eats that one. Something else can travel the same road, and it does something energy does not: it builds up.

Some substances are toxic, which means they damage living things. A few reach a habitat by accident and some are put there on purpose - a pesticide sprayed on a crop, waste tipped into a river, mercury washed out of mining. The important point is what happens next. Many of these substances are not broken down by a living body and are not passed out in its waste. They stay in the body, usually in its fat, for the rest of its life.

Now follow the chain. A tiny amount of poison in the water is taken up by the algae - so little in each one that it would be hard to measure. A small fish eats thousands of algae in its life, and keeps the poison from every one of them, so the fish now carries thousands of times the dose. A larger fish eats dozens of those small fish, and keeps all of theirs. A fish eagle eats many of the larger fish. At each step the poison is concentrated, because the eater is keeping everything its food had collected, and this is called bioaccumulation.

That is why the animals at the top of a chain are harmed first and worst, even though they never went near the source. A fish eagle can be poisoned by a spray applied to a field it never flew over, carried down a stream it never drank from. It also explains something that surprises people: a level of pollution far too low to hurt anything in the water can still be lethal four steps up.

Humans sit at the top of many food chains, which is why advice about how much of certain large fish is safe to eat exists at all. It is not the fish that is unusual. It is that a large, long-lived predator has had time to collect what everything below it collected first.
concepts.example: A pesticide is used on farmland beside a lake at a concentration measured in parts per billion - far too weak to harm the algae it settles on. Ten years later the lake's fish eagles are laying eggs with shells too thin to survive being sat on. Nothing in the lake got more polluted; the poison simply travelled up four steps, and each step multiplied it.

concepts.title: Temperature Changes What Dissolves, and How Much
concepts.explanation:
You have seen that a solid can dissolve in water to make a solution, and that it has not disappeared - it is still there in pieces too small to see. Now the question a cook already knows the answer to: does temperature make any difference?

It makes two. The first is speed. Stir a spoonful of sugar into cold water and into hot water, and the hot one clears much sooner. The second is quantity, and it is the more surprising one: hot water will dissolve MORE sugar than cold water will. Keep adding sugar to cold water and there comes a point where no more will go in however long you stir - the solution is saturated, and any extra sits on the bottom. Warm that same glass and the sugar on the bottom disappears. There was room for more all along; the water just had to be warmer to make it.

The particle model explains both. In a liquid the particles are always moving, and warming them makes them move faster. Faster-moving water particles collide with the sugar more often and more heftily, so they knock its particles loose from the lump more quickly - that is the speed. They also spread further apart as they move faster, leaving more gaps for the sugar particles to fit into - that is the quantity.

The effect runs backwards too, and it is worth watching for. A hot saturated solution that cools cannot hold everything it was holding, so the extra comes back out of the solution as solid. Sugar crystals appearing at the bottom of a jar of cooled syrup are not sugar that was never dissolved. They are sugar that was dissolved, and was pushed back out when the water cooled and no longer had room.
concepts.example: Two glasses hold 100 ml of water, one cold and one hot, and you add sugar a spoon at a time until no more will dissolve. The cold glass stops taking it after about two spoons; the hot glass keeps going for far longer. Let the hot one stand overnight and you find sugar on the bottom in the morning - the same sugar, put back out as the water cooled.

concepts.title: Boiling and Evaporation Are Not the Same Thing
concepts.explanation:
Both turn a liquid into a gas, and it is easy to think they are one process at different speeds. They are not, and the differences are worth having straight.

Evaporation happens at the SURFACE, at any temperature, and it happens all the time. A puddle dries on a cool morning; washing dries on a line without anyone heating it. Only the particles at the surface that happen to be moving fastest escape into the air, which is why it is slow, and why warmth, wind and a wide shallow shape all speed it up - more surface, and more fast particles.

Boiling happens THROUGHOUT the liquid, and only at one particular temperature. Bubbles of gas form deep in the pan, not just at the top, and rise - which is what you are looking at when you say water is boiling. It cannot happen at all below that temperature, and once it starts the temperature stops climbing however hard you heat: extra energy goes into turning liquid into gas rather than into making it hotter.

That particular temperature is the second idea here, and it is a property of the substance itself. Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level and melts at 0. Those numbers are not facts about your pan; they are facts about water, as much a property of it as its being clear or its dissolving salt. Every substance has its own pair. Iron melts at about 1538 degrees and pure gold at about 1064, which is why a goldsmith's furnace need not be as fierce as a blacksmith's. Oxygen melts at minus 219, which is why you have never seen a piece of it.

Because the numbers belong to the substance, they can be used to identify it - and to check its purity, since dissolving something in a liquid shifts them. Salted water boils a degree or two above 100, which is a small effect and a real one.
concepts.example: A pan of water is heated with a thermometer in it. The reading climbs steadily to 100 degrees and then stops, and stays at 100 for the whole time the water is boiling away, even though the flame has not been turned down. The energy is still going in; it is going into the change of state rather than into the temperature.

concepts.title: A Gas Has Mass, and You Can Weigh It
concepts.explanation:
Air feels like nothing. You walk through it, you cannot see it, and an empty-looking bag seems to weigh the same whether it is open or closed. It is easy to conclude that a gas has no mass at all - and that conclusion is wrong, which matters, because it is the last place people stop believing that gases are properly matter.

A gas is made of particles, like a solid or a liquid, and every particle has mass. There are simply far fewer of them in the same space: the particles in a gas are spread out with a great deal of nothing between them, where the particles in a solid are packed against each other. So the same volume holds much less material, and that is why a gas feels like nothing rather than being nothing. A cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms - roughly a large bottle of water, in the space above your desk.

You can show it with a balance. Weigh a sealed football that has been pumped hard, then let some air out and weigh it again: it is lighter, and nothing has left it but gas. Or weigh a closed bottle, open it and let the gas from a fizzy drink escape, and watch the reading fall. The mass did not vanish - it drifted off into the room.

This is also why the difference between a full and an empty gas cylinder can be felt by anyone who has carried one, and why a hot-air balloon rises: the air inside has been warmed, its particles have spread further apart, so the same volume now holds fewer particles and therefore less mass than the cold air outside. The balloon does not become weightless. It becomes lighter than the air it displaces, which is a different and more useful thing.
concepts.example: A football is weighed on a kitchen balance at 445 grams, hard-pumped. Air is let out until it is soft, and it weighs 442 grams. Three grams of air have left the ball - a mass you cannot feel and can certainly measure.

concepts.title: Why a Ship Floats and a Coin Sinks
concepts.explanation:
Ask why something floats and the first answer is usually that it is light. It is a reasonable guess and it cannot be right, because a steel ship weighing thousands of tonnes floats while a steel coin weighing a few grams goes straight to the bottom. Mass alone does not decide it. Shape is doing something.

When you put an object in water it pushes some water out of the way, and the water pushes back up on the object. That upward push is called upthrust, and how big it is depends on how much water the object shoves aside. Put the coin in and it shoves aside only a coin's worth of water - a tiny volume, so a tiny upthrust, far less than the coin's weight pulling down. Down it goes.

Now take the same amount of steel and beat it into a wide hollow hull. It now occupies an enormous volume, most of it air, and when it settles into the water it shoves aside a huge amount. The upthrust grows until it equals the ship's weight, and at that point the ship stops sinking and floats. Nothing about the steel changed. What changed is how much water the shape displaces.

So the rule is a comparison, not a single quantity: an object floats if it can displace a weight of water equal to its own weight before it goes under. That is why mass and shape are both in the answer, and why either one alone misleads. A solid lump of steel cannot displace enough and sinks; the same steel as a bowl can and floats. It is also why an overloaded boat sinks - adding cargo adds weight without adding any more hull to displace with, until the two can no longer balance.
concepts.example: A ball of modelling clay dropped in a bowl of water sinks at once. Lift it out, press it into a wide shallow dish shape and set it on the water, and it floats - carrying several coins before it goes under. Same clay, same mass, different amount of water shoved aside.

concepts.title: The Same Metals Carry Heat
concepts.explanation:
You have sorted materials into conductors and insulators by whether they let electricity through. Now try the same materials with something else entirely: heat. The answer is that the sorting comes out almost the same, and that is not a coincidence.

Stand a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in a mug of hot water and come back in two minutes. The metal handle is hot to hold and the wooden one is barely warm. Heat has travelled up the metal and has hardly moved through the wood. A material that carries heat well is a thermal conductor; one that does not is a thermal insulator. Metals are good thermal conductors. Wood, plastic, cloth, air and water are poor ones.

That is the same list as for electricity, and the reason is that in a metal some electrons are not tied to any one atom and are free to move through the whole piece. Push them with a cell and you get an electric current. Warm one end and those same loose electrons carry the energy along as they move, which is why the far end heats up so quickly. In wood or plastic nothing is free to travel, so neither electricity nor heat gets far.

Both kinds of conductivity are properties of the substance, like its melting point: copper conducts heat and electricity well wherever you find it, and being told a material is copper tells you both. That is why the two words get used together, and why it is worth naming which one you mean.

It also explains a great deal of ordinary equipment. A cooking pot is metal so the heat reaches the food, with a wooden or plastic handle so it does not reach your hand. The two materials are chosen for opposite reasons in the same object.
concepts.example: A metal teaspoon and a plastic one are stood in the same mug of hot water for two minutes. The metal one cannot be held comfortably; the plastic one can. The water was the same temperature for both, so the difference is entirely in what the spoon is made of.

concepts.title: Two Ways to Wire Two Lamps
concepts.explanation:
Everything you have built so far has been a series circuit: one loop, with the cell and every component on it, so the same current passes through each in turn. Add a second lamp to a series circuit and both lamps go dim, because that one current now has two lamps to push through instead of one. Unscrew either lamp and the other goes out - the loop is broken and nothing can flow anywhere.

There is another way to wire them. In a parallel circuit the current leaves the cell and the path SPLITS, one branch through each lamp, and the branches join again before returning. Now each lamp has its own route back to the cell. Two consequences follow, and they are what makes parallel worth knowing.

The first is brightness. Each lamp in a parallel circuit gets the cell's full push, so both are as bright as a single lamp on its own - much brighter than the same two lamps in series. The cell pays for this by supplying more current altogether and running down faster.

The second is independence. Unscrew one lamp in a parallel circuit and the other stays lit, because its own branch is untouched. That is why a house is wired in parallel: a room's light failing does not darken the rest of the house, and each lamp receives the full mains voltage rather than a share of it. String lights of the old kind were wired in series, which is why one dead bulb used to put out the whole string.

So the choice is a real engineering decision. Series is simpler and uses less wire, and everything on it shares one current and one fate. Parallel costs more wire and gives every component full brightness and a life of its own.
concepts.example: Two identical lamps are wired in series with one cell, and both glow faintly. The same two lamps and the same cell are rewired in parallel, and both glow brightly. Unscrewing one now leaves the other burning - in the series circuit it had put both out.
